analysis.one_liner: Removes the health insurance industry's federal antitrust exemption so competition laws apply.
analysis.headline: The bill to end health insurers' antitrust exemption never got a vote; it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Health insurers are currently shielded from most federal antitrust laws by a 1945 law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act, which lets states regulate insurance instead of the federal government. This bill would say that shield does not apply to health insurance, so federal antitrust laws — including bans on unfair methods of competition — would fully apply to health insurers. That means the Justice Department and the FTC could go after price-fixing, market allocation, and other anti-competitive conduct by health insurance companies.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy health insurance — through employers, on their own, or through public programs run through private insurers — would benefit if insurers face the same competition laws as most other industries. Small businesses and consumers paying premiums in heavily consolidated insurance markets could see lower prices and more choices if anti-competitive mergers or collusion were challenged.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health insurance customers and small employers

how_it_helps.text: Strips health insurance of the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, making federal laws against monopolization and collusion fully enforceable against health insurers.
Applies the ban on unfair methods of competition to health insurance regardless of whether the insurer operates for profit, covering nonprofit insurer conduct as well.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance companies, both for-profit and nonprofit, would bear the cost of antitrust exposure — potential lawsuits, damages, and lost ability to coordinate pricing. Consumers could ultimately bear some of any compliance costs passed into premiums.

drawbacks.text: Insurers warned that antitrust exposure, including potential treble-damage lawsuits, could raise compliance costs that get passed to consumers as higher premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — subjecting one of the most consolidated consumer industries to competition law like everyone else — is broad but indirect; premiums might not fall quickly, and enforcement depends on regulators acting. The cost falls on insurers, though some could be passed to premium payers. Most economists would call the trade favorable to consumers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee on antitrust matters in February 2013, and no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch introduced the bill on January 22, 2013, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On February 28, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law.
No markup, floor vote, or further action ever occurred before the 113th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurance companies kept the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption that shields them from federal competition law, and no congressional action disturbed that status quo during the two-year Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurance companies kept their antitrust shield

for.name: Rep. Stephen Lynch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip health insurers of the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members are in the record — the Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor — and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: Would lose the McCarran-Ferguson antitrust exemption, exposing insurers to federal antitrust enforcement for collusion, anti-competitive mergers, and unfair methods of competition, including nonprofit insurers. Industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs against consumers paying premiums in consolidated markets.

industries.industry: Consumers and small businesses buying health insurance
industries.note: Would benefit from potential enforcement against anti-competitive conduct in consolidated insurance markets, possibly lowering premiums or increasing plan choice.
